newsitem.title: USA: Sunbeam reports a loss; plans big restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Sunbeam reports a loss; plans big restructuring.

text.p: Sunbeam Corp., the ailing appliance maker, Wednesday reported a loss for the latest quarter -- its first downturn since going public in 1992 -- and announced that it plans a "massive" restructuring.
The company said it lost $28.7 million, or 22 cents a share, in the third quarter, compared with a profit of $15.0 million, or 11 cents a share, a year ago.
Sales were down 2 percent to $244.9 million, from $250.7 million in last year's third quarter.
"We are focusing all of our energies on restructuring Sunbeam and creating a dramatically different company going forward," said Albert J. Dunlap, chairman and chief executive.
"We expect to announce the restructuring plan, in detail, during the week of November 11th, after approval of the plan by our board of directors," he said.
Sunbeam, which has a work force of 12,000 and annual sales of $1 billion, has seen its profits dwindle in recent years due to shrinking profit margins and high manufacturing and administrative costs.
It sells appliances under the Sunbeam and Oster brand names, including home appliances, outdoor furniture, health and beauty appliances, clocks and bathroom scales.
Last year it earned $50.5 million, less than half its 1994 earnings.

"The results for the quarter, as expected, continue to reflect the inflated cost structure and the lack of an appropriate growth strategy that have plagued the company for the past two years," Dunlap said.
"The financial performance over this period highlights why my new management team and I recently joined Sunbeam -- to implement a rapid and massive restructuring," he said.
Dunlap, who is widely known as "Chainsaw Al" for his slash-and-burn tactics in corporate restructuring, has a reputation for helping ailing companies rebound.
He was named chairman and chief executive of Sunbeam on July 18, and has promised to overhaul the firm within a year.
Dunlap is credited with turning around Scott Paper Co., which was eventually sold to Kimberly-Clark, and Lily-Tulip Inc.
During his stay at Scott Paper, Dunlap fired 10,000 workers and sold more than $2 billion in assets.
Dunlap has said that he would review Sunbeam's product line with an eye to eliminating less-profitable items.
Within months of joining Sunbeam, he replaced several top executives, brought in people who have worked for him in the past and credited new posts.
Sunbeam's stock was off 12.5 cents at $24.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
